None of our experiments has varied muon_newton_schulz_steps, so our world models have no evidence on this proposed change: Time lever at near-equal math, the one Muon-cost cut not yet tried. Start from tip E031 (commit 3797e1a). First read the Newton-Schulz iteration count in the code. Then profile about 50 steps at each resolution on synthetic data with torch.profiler, recording the NS bmm share per step; this answers H2.4.3 without a separate run. Then change only the iteration count: 5 -> 3 if the code runs 5, othe What does the literature say about its effect in settings like ours, and what mechanism decides it? Our world models believe:
  W31 (replays 90%; premise: Prefer the simplest model that fits: each setting moves each metric by a fixed amount or f): Time is steps times a per-step cost: width-driven per-sample compute plus about 12% fixed per-step overhead, so smaller batches are slower per sample. Low-res phases cut pixel compute (24px about 0.56x, 28px about 0.77x). Muon adds fixed time but gains accuracy. Accuracy rises with epochs and width. Cutout, translate4, random flip, off-optimal label smoothing and low-res phases cost accuracy. E016 looks like an outlier (noise or glitch), so it is not modeled.
  W32 (replays 93%; premise: Assume what this literature digest (D007) reports holds in this task, and build on it:
# D): Time = fixed ~0.7s + steps × per-step cost. Per-step cost is affine in stage widths (c1, c2 dominate; c3 cheap), sublinear in batch (~bs^0.8), reduced by low-res phases (~78% of pixel-ratio saving), plus Muon overhead. Accuracy rises with epochs (saturating), width, and Muon (+0.8pt). It falls with cutout, translate4, random flip, label smoothing away from 0.1, and low-res phases (~0.5pt).
  W33 (replays 93%; premise: Account for the objective as the sum of the costs of the process's parts. Derive each part): Time is steps times per-step cost: a fixed launch/optimizer overhead, Muon overhead, and a batch-proportional term made of a small constant plus conv FLOPs (from channel widths) scaled by the resolution curriculum, where low-res steps cost about half. plan.question: How does the Newton-Schulz iteration count in Muon (e.g. 5 -> 3, or fewer with per-iteration-optimized coefficients) affect accuracy per step and wall-clock time in short, small-model training runs such as an ~200-step, batch-2048 CIFAR conv net? What mechanism decides whether looser orthogonalization is harmless? Candidates are the singular-value spread of the momentum matrix for small, wide conv filters (e.g. 704x6336), the changed effective update RMS (a hidden lr change), bf16 precision, and whether approximate orthogonalization acts as a useful regularizer. Also, what share of per-step time does NS take in practice?
queries: Polar Express optimal polynomial Newton-Schulz Muon
Muon optimizer convolution small batch speedrun CIFAR
inexact polar decomposition optimizer update RMS spectral norm
rubric: Varies the Newton-Schulz (or polar-approximation) iteration count or polynomial and reports the effect on training loss or accuracy at a fixed step count or a fixed budget
Reports the wall-clock or FLOP cost of the orthogonalization step relative to the total step time, or measures cost on small matrices or conv filters
Explains a mechanism for the accuracy effect, such as singular-value spread after the iterations, update-norm or RMS change acting as an lr change, or bf16 numerical error
Setting is short-horizon or small-model training (CIFAR or speedrun-scale, or small LM), or gives results that transfer to it
exclude: Pretrained weights, fine-tuning or transfer learning from external data
Test-time augmentation or any use of the test set during training
Methods requiring packages beyond PyTorch 2.4.0 / torchvision 0.19.0
Large-scale distributed Muon systems papers that only address communication or sharding cost
Second-order methods with full-matrix preconditioners (Shampoo/SOAP) unless they directly compare NS iteration counts
